claims.text: Adding boron during laser cladding causes in situ formation of distributed boride phases in the HEA matrix.
The boride phases are finely dispersed precipitates.
Boron-induced boride phases increase coating hardness.
Boron-induced boride phases promote a more stable or more effectively passivated surface.
The simultaneous effects on hardness and passivation govern the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
Compared with an otherwise matched boron-free coating, the boron-enriched coating will have lower wear-volume loss under identical tribo-corrosion conditions.
Compared with an otherwise matched boron-free coating, the boron-enriched coating will have lower corrosion-current density under identical tribo-corrosion conditions.
The combined reductions in wear and corrosion will lower total degradation during tribo-corrosion.
The proposed benefit should hold in mildly corrosive chloride solutions where a passive film can form and remain stable.
The proposed benefit may fail at very high acidity or high temperature.
The proposed benefit may fail when mechanical stress continuously disrupts the passive film.
The boron-added and boron-free coatings should be compared under identical chloride-containing aqueous tribo-corrosion conditions at ambient temperature.
Wear loss, corrosion-current density, passivation behavior, and boride-phase formation and distribution can be measured to test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in both wear-volume loss and corrosion-current density relative to the baseline is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
Failure to observe the expected boride phases is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
